source.title: Symbolic Rule Extraction from Attention-Guided Sparse Representations in Vision Transformers

record.file_problem: The full paper text and appendix are present. The publication metadata in the header is inconsistent with the supplied venue and year, but the text is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports that some neurons in its ViT representation do not show clear concept selectivity, refining claims about neuron interpretability. It does not measure the audit shares or the explanation-prediction tests in the other versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports classification accuracy and rule-set size results, but these do not measure neuron interpretability. The relevant results are its qualitative inspection of selected neurons' activation heatmaps and concept labels.
record.test_reason: The study trains a new sparse, binarized concept head on ViT-Base with L1, entropy and supervised contrastive losses, so concept selectivity is induced on purpose rather than measured in the model's native neurons. Its interpretability evidence is three hand-picked neurons from one dataset (P3.1), shown qualitatively. It reports no share of interpretable neurons and does not compare tools or architectures. It relies on neurons mapping to concepts as the basis for its semantic-labelling step, and its quantitative results concern its own method's accuracy and rule-set size. So it bears on none of V1–V7, including V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors' main conclusion is that NeSyViT extracts concise rule-sets: 67% smaller than NeSyFOLD on average, with a 5.14% average accuracy gain over vanilla ViT. On interpretability, they say the CNN-derived automatic labelling struggles in ViTs because neuron monosemanticity is limited. They add that heatmaps allow manual inspection, and they leave better disentanglement and monosemanticity to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a sparse, binarized concept layer on ViT-Base and inspects selected neuron heatmaps; it does not use the Qwen neuron-pole audit or held-out activation-prediction scoring described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper says semantic labelling adapted from CNN work is less reliable in ViTs; it does not report a controlled comparison across tools, architectures, or settings for neuron selectivity.

fits_no_version.finding: In a ViT-Base head trained with sparsity, entropy and contrastive losses, one of three displayed rule neurons (106, 'bed') is concept-selective. Neurons 43 and 105 respond to mixed features. The authors say IoU-based automatic labelling 'struggles in ViTs due to limited neuron monosemanticity'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In sparsity-trained concept layers on ViTs, segmentation-IoU labelling of top-activating images yields unreliable concept labels for some neurons.

record.peer_reviewed: Theory and Practice of Logic Programming 25 (2025), 722–738
record.problems: The interpretability evidence is qualitative and limited to selected neurons and a P3.1 example; the paper gives no quantified neuron-level selectivity rate or uncertainty for these observations. It does not test explanations on held-out activating examples.
record.rows_left_out: Classification accuracy, rule-set size, and rule-set examples are not neuron-selectivity measurements and were left out.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and no job-count shares.
No language models, mixture-of-experts models or scaling; only one ViT-Base head.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose or recursive generalization analysis.
No estimate of the share of interpretable native neurons, and no comparison of tools, architectures or regularization effects on that share.
No attribution graphs and no comparison with a replacement model.
No test of whether explanations derived from top-activating examples predict where neurons fire.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 limits_scope label is dropped. The layer is engineered for selectivity, only three neurons are shown, and no share or tool comparison is reported, so it cannot qualify V4's claim about interpretable shares in native neurons.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or estimate the shares with one, two, or unknown jobs.
Uses one ViT-Base configuration and does not test other models, mixture-of-experts, or scaling to larger models.
Does not study InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron, pose, or recursive generalization.

Inspects selected neurons in a trained ViT setting but does not estimate the overall share of interpretable neurons, compare architectures or tool quality, or test the stated InceptionV1-sized model estimates.
Does not evaluate attribution graphs or compare neuron-based explanations with a trained replacement model.
Does not test explanations against held-out activating examples or measure whether they predict firing.
Does not score explanations by simulating neuron activations on new text.

rows.size_stated: ViT-Base; sparse concept layer output dimension 128
rows.stage_stated: ImageNet-1k pretrained weights; trained for 50 epochs with supervised contrastive, entropy, and L1 sparsity losses
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the activation heatmap and semantic association of neuron 106

conditions.value: top-5 images visualized; semantic labelling uses top-10 activating images

rows.measure: Qualitative concept selectivity in activation heatmaps
rows.value: Neuron 106 consistently activates for the bed concept in bedroom images.
rows.note: This is a qualitative result for a selected neuron, not an estimate of the share of interpretable neurons.
rows.check: The neuron belongs to a purpose-trained sparse concept head, not native model neurons, and is one hand-selected example. It gives no share and no tool or architecture comparison, so it cannot bear on V4. Qualitatively, neuron 106 is selective for 'bed'.
